title: New on the payroll, and the name appears somewhere close by
question: Which new entrants share a rare name with someone a candidate’s campaign had been paying, a recent commissioner of the same department, or an officer of an organization the department funds?
finding: 21 new entrants carry a rare name that also appears in a connected record: 14 were paid as campaign staff or consultants by the committee of an elected official in whose department they then started (Board of Supervisors: 8, Mayor: 4, Sheriff: 1, District Attorney: 1), 3 had been paid as a board or commission member under the department that then put them on staff, and 4 of the 7 people already listed as coming from a funded organization started in the best-paid twentieth. 5 of the 21 started in the best-paid twentieth. Every row is a name match with a second link, not a confirmed identity.
how: Names are matched under the rules of the people screens: one spelling and one person in the payroll, and rare (fewer than one other Bay Area resident expected to share it); 48,514 of 71,958 payroll names pass. Campaign: payments to an individual coded as campaign workers’ salaries or campaign consultants on the expenditure schedules of a committee controlled by a candidate, totalling $1,000 or more in the five years before the end of the person’s first City fiscal year, where that candidate is on the City payroll as an elected official in the department that hired the person, within a year of the hire. Board seat: the same name paid in a board or commission class under a department in an earlier fiscal year than its first staff pay of $20,000 or more in that department. Funded organization: rows of the existing screen, kept here only when the first City job was in the best-paid twentieth. New entrants are names first seen in fiscal 2019 or later. The last column states the rule that governs the type of appointment the payroll records.
limits: People who worked on a campaign are an ordinary source of aides for the official who won, and the payroll records every campaign-linked post here as an exempt appointment, the kind the City Charter excludes from competitive selection. Commissioners know the department and may apply for its jobs; whether any waiting rule applies is for the Ethics Commission to say. A rare name can still belong to two people. The campaign file names only people the committee paid directly, so staff paid through a payroll company or a consulting firm do not appear. What would settle each row is the job announcement, the list of candidates and the appointment form.
